stem: A 44-year-old woman presents to your general practice concerned about a 12 kg weight gain over 6 months despite unchanged diet. She has developed acne, easy bruising on her forearms and reports low mood. On examination she has central obesity, wide purple striae on her abdomen and a rounded plethoric face. Her BP is 158/94. She is not on exogenous steroids and works day shifts as an accountant with a regular sleep schedule. Fasting glucose is 8.1 mmol/L on today's finger-prick test.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 158/94, RR 14, SpO2 99 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Central obesity, moon facies, dorsocervical fat pad, wide purple striae on abdomen; proximal muscle weakness on rising from chair without arms; supraclavicular fullness
data_table.Investigations: Fasting glucose 8.1 mmol/L (<7.0), HbA1c 6.8 percent (<5.7); TSH 2.1 mIU/L; UEC and calcium within normal limits; not on exogenous glucocorticoids; not pregnant

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial screening test?

options.text: Serum ACTH morning level with paired cortisol as the initial screening test, expecting an elevated ACTH to indicate pituitary Cushing and a suppressed ACTH to indicate adrenal Cushing directly
options.rationale: ACTH is used to distinguish ACTH-dependent from ACTH-independent Cushing after screening confirms hypercortisolism; not the first screen.

options.text: Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test with a morning serum cortisol at 8 am, considering a cortisol below 50 nmol/L as an adequate response and above 50 nmol/L as an abnormal screen
options.rationale: 1 mg overnight dexamethasone suppression test is a first-line Endocrine Society AU-endorsed screen for Cushing syndrome; morning cortisol above 50 nmol/L is abnormal and prompts confirmatory testing.

options.text: Single 8 am morning serum cortisol level, with a value above the upper limit of normal (over 550 nmol/L) considered diagnostic of Cushing syndrome and prompting immediate imaging referral
options.rationale: Single morning cortisol has poor discrimination for Cushing; loss of diurnal rhythm and failure to suppress on DST are the screening tests.

options.text: Serum aldosterone-to-renin ratio measured in the morning after 2 hours upright posture as the initial screen given the hypertension and hypokalaemia are commonly associated with primary aldosteronism
options.rationale: ARR screens for primary aldosteronism, not Cushing; her clinical features (central obesity, striae, proximal weakness, plethora) point to Cushing.

options.text: MRI pituitary with dynamic contrast enhancement as the initial investigation given the classical clinical picture is highly suggestive of pituitary adenoma causing Cushing disease in this scenario today
options.rationale: Imaging follows biochemical confirmation; up to 10 percent of the population has incidental pituitary microadenomas so pre-biochemistry MRI misleads.

explanation.summary: Suspected Cushing syndrome is screened with one of three first-line tests: overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test, 24-hour urinary free cortisol (two collections), or late-night salivary cortisol (two samples). A positive screen requires a second abnormal test from the panel to confirm hypercortisolism before proceeding to ACTH and localisation. Single morning cortisol and pituitary MRI are not initial screens because they lack specificity or lead to incidentalomas.
key_points: 1 mg overnight DST is a first-line Cushing screen
Alternatives: 24 hr UFC (x2), late-night salivary cortisol (x2)
Need two abnormal tests before diagnostic confirmation
ACTH and imaging follow biochemical confirmation, not precede it
explanation.pearls: Common causes of false-positive DST include pregnancy, oestrogen therapy (raises CBG), rifampicin (accelerates dexamethasone metabolism), depression, chronic alcohol use and severe illness; check for these before pursuing confirmatory workup on an isolated abnormal screen.

stem: A 68-year-old post-menopausal woman is referred to your general practice for review after a low-trauma wrist fracture 4 weeks ago from a fall from standing height. She smokes 10 cigarettes daily, drinks 3 standard drinks daily and has been on prednisolone 7.5 mg orally daily for polymyalgia rheumatica for 8 months. Her DEXA scan shows lumbar spine T-score -2.8 and femoral neck T-score -2.5. Her mother had a hip fracture at age 74. Her calcium and vitamin D are within normal limits.

data_table.Examination: Mildly kyphotic thoracic spine; no acute back tenderness; no visible dental disease; no active infection
data_table.Investigations: DEXA lumbar T -2.8, femoral neck T -2.5; calcium 2.36 mmol/L (2.15 to 2.55), 25-OH vitamin D 68 nmol/L (>=50), eGFR 76 mL/min/1.73 m2; PTH 3.8 pmol/L (1.6 to 7.2), TSH 2.1 mIU/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line pharmacotherapy?

options.text: IV zoledronic acid 5 mg once yearly infusion as first-line pharmacotherapy as she has ongoing steroid exposure, and no dental review or renal check is required as her eGFR is above 35 mL/min
options.rationale: IV zoledronate is used when oral bisphosphonates are not tolerated or absorbed; oral alendronate is first-line in AU. Dental review remains prudent before any bisphosphonate.

options.text: Denosumab 60 mg subcutaneous every 6 months as first-line pharmacotherapy without any prior bisphosphonate trial and without long-term commitment to a follow-on antiresorptive after eventual cessation
options.rationale: Denosumab is a valid option but not first-line before an oral bisphosphonate trial; and it must be followed by a bisphosphonate on cessation to prevent rebound vertebral fractures, requiring long-term planning.

options.text: Teriparatide 20 microgram subcutaneous daily for 18 months as first-line anabolic therapy given the very low T-scores and glucocorticoid use as the anabolic pathway is more effective than antiresorptive
options.rationale: Teriparatide is used after antiresorptive failure or in severe osteoporosis with vertebral fractures; not first-line, is limited on PBS to specific criteria, and has an 18 to 24 month lifetime cap.

options.text: Oral alendronate 70 mg weekly on an empty stomach with 200 mL water and remain upright for 30 minutes, calcium and vitamin D optimisation, dental review before starting, and 5-year review
options.rationale: Post-menopausal osteoporosis with prior fragility fracture is a clear indication for oral bisphosphonate; alendronate is first-line PBS-listed with dental review before initiation for MRONJ risk mitigation.

options.text: Increase oral calcium to 1500 mg daily plus vitamin D 2000 IU daily and lifestyle modification alone for 12 months, review DEXA at 12 months before considering any specific antiresorptive therapy
options.rationale: Calcium and vitamin D alone do not reduce fracture risk sufficiently in established osteoporosis after fragility fracture; pharmacotherapy is required.

explanation.summary: Post-menopausal osteoporosis with a fragility fracture, T-score <=-2.5 at hip or spine, or chronic glucocorticoid exposure warrants first-line oral bisphosphonate therapy (alendronate 70 mg weekly or risedronate 35 mg weekly) with calcium and vitamin D optimisation, dental review to reduce MRONJ risk, and 5-yearly reassessment. IV zoledronate is second-line for intolerance. Denosumab is an alternative but requires follow-on antiresorptive on cessation. Teriparatide is reserved for severe or bisphosphonate-refractory disease.
key_points: First-line pharmacotherapy: oral alendronate or risedronate
Dental review before bisphosphonate for MRONJ risk mitigation
IV zoledronate second-line if oral intolerance
Denosumab needs follow-on bisphosphonate to prevent rebound fractures
explanation.pearls: Bisphosphonate holiday after 5 years of oral therapy is considered for low-risk patients but not for those with continuing high risk (prior vertebral fracture, femoral neck T -2.5, ongoing glucocorticoid use); a repeat DEXA and clinical assessment guide the decision.

subtopic_detail: Endocarditis Duke criteria and empiric therapy
stem: A 62-year-old man presents to your emergency department with 2 weeks of intermittent fevers, night sweats and 4 kg weight loss. He had a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement 3 months ago. On examination he has a new soft early diastolic murmur, splinter haemorrhages under two fingernails and tender nodules on the pulp of his index finger. Three sets of blood cultures drawn 1 hour apart are all positive for Streptococcus gallolyticus (bovis). Transthoracic echo shows a mobile 1.2 cm echogenic mass on the aortic prosthesis with mild aortic regurgitation.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 132/62, RR 18, SpO2 96 percent, temp 38.4 C
data_table.Examination: Splinter haemorrhages under two fingernails; tender pulp nodules on index finger (Osler nodes); new soft early diastolic aortic murmur; no peripheral oedema
data_table.Investigations: Blood cultures x3 all positive S. gallolyticus; TTE 1.2 cm mobile aortic prosthesis vegetation; mild AR; CRP 92 mg/L (<5); WCC 15 x10^9/L; creatinine 92 micromol/L

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management combination?

options.text: IV vancomycin 25 mg/kg loading then 15 mg/kg every 12 hours monotherapy for 6 weeks and defer any surgical review or transoesophageal echo pending clinical improvement over the next 5 to 7 days
options.rationale: Vancomycin monotherapy is not optimal for penicillin-susceptible streptococcal endocarditis and delaying TOE plus surgical consult in prosthetic valve endocarditis with regurgitation risks disease progression.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g daily monotherapy for 4 weeks and observation without cardiothoracic surgical consultation as vegetations under 2 cm rarely embolise and the mild aortic regurgitation is stable
options.rationale: Prosthetic valve endocarditis warrants combination therapy with gentamicin for 2 to 6 weeks under AU guidelines; and cardiothoracic surgical consultation is mandatory in prosthetic valve endocarditis for shared surgical decision making.

options.text: IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g every 4 hours plus IV gentamicin 3 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks total, arrange transoesophageal echo, colonoscopy for occult colorectal malignancy and cardiothoracic surgery review
options.rationale: This meets modified Duke definite endocarditis (two major: positive typical organism and vegetation on echo); AU regimen for streptococcal PVE is benzylpenicillin plus low-dose gentamicin; S. gallolyticus mandates colonoscopy for occult colorectal cancer.

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 4 hours plus IV rifampicin 600 mg orally twice daily for suspected staphylococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis empirically before waiting for the confirmed culture identification
options.rationale: Culture is confirmed as S. gallolyticus, not S. aureus; flucloxacillin does not cover streptococci and rifampicin is only added for staphylococcal PVE, not streptococcal.

options.text: Broad-spectrum empirical piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours pending susceptibility results, with home IV therapy commenced through the outpatient antimicrobial program once afebrile for 48 hours
options.rationale: PVE in the first 12 months post surgery does not have the microbiology of community endocarditis and needs inpatient management for at least the first 2 weeks per AU guidance; and piperacillin-tazobactam is not the streptococcal PVE regimen.

explanation.summary: Modified Duke criteria diagnose definite infective endocarditis when there are 2 major (typical organism in 2+ blood cultures, echocardiographic evidence of endocardial involvement), or 1 major plus 3 minor, or 5 minor criteria. AU regimen for streptococcal prosthetic valve endocarditis is benzylpenicillin 2.4 g IV every 4 hours plus low-dose gentamicin 3 mg/kg daily for 6 weeks. Prosthetic valve endocarditis mandates transoesophageal echocardiogram, cardiothoracic surgical review and colonoscopy for S. gallolyticus.
key_points: Modified Duke: 2 major, or 1 major + 3 minor, or 5 minor = definite
Streptococcal PVE: benzylpenicillin + gentamicin 6 weeks
S. gallolyticus mandates colonoscopy for occult colorectal cancer
PVE always needs TOE and cardiothoracic surgical review
explanation.pearls: Surgical indications for infective endocarditis include heart failure from valve dysfunction, uncontrolled infection despite adequate antibiotics after 5 to 7 days, large vegetations (>10 mm) with embolic phenomena and paravalvular abscess or dehiscence; early surgery in the first week improves outcomes when these are present.

stem: A 43-year-old woman with a background of Hashimoto thyroiditis on levothyroxine presents to your emergency department with 2 days of vomiting, abdominal pain and profound fatigue. She has felt increasingly weak, dizzy on standing and salt-craving over 3 months. She is otherwise on no medications. On examination she has hyperpigmentation of her palmar creases, buccal mucosa and recent surgical scar from an appendicectomy 10 years ago. Blood pressure is 78/48 mmHg. She is severely dehydrated and has never taken glucocorticoids.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 78/48, RR 22, SpO2 98 percent, temp 36.7 C
data_table.Examination: Hyperpigmented palmar creases, buccal mucosa, old surgical scar; dry mucous membranes; supine BP drops from 92 to 78/48 on sitting; peripherally cool; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L (135 to 145), K 5.8 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), glucose 3.2 mmol/L (3.5 to 5.5), urea 12 mmol/L, creatinine 108 micromol/L, TSH 4.8 mIU/L (0.4 to 4.0), VBG pH 7.32; morning cortisol pending

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV dexamethasone 4 mg stat before drawing morning cortisol and ACTH samples, IV Hartmann 1000 mL over the first hour and observe supine BP before further pharmacological intervention
options.rationale: Hartmann contains potassium which may worsen hyperkalaemia in acute adrenal crisis; and dexamethasone lacks mineralocorticoid activity so hydrocortisone is preferred.

options.text: Increase levothyroxine to 200 microgram orally daily for suspected myxoedema coma, IV normal saline 500 mL over 30 minutes and cover with ceftriaxone 2 g pending source review of infection today
options.rationale: Increasing levothyroxine before glucocorticoid replacement in adrenal insufficiency precipitates further crisis by increasing cortisol clearance; hydrocortisone must be given first.

options.text: IV insulin actrapid 5 unit and 50 mL 50 percent dextrose for hyperkalaemia, IV calcium gluconate 10 mL 10 percent for cardioprotection and IV frusemide 40 mg for potassium excretion while awaiting cortisol
options.rationale: Insulin risks worsening hypoglycaemia in a hypoglycaemic patient; the definitive treatment is hydrocortisone and saline which correct all three electrolyte and glucose derangements.

options.text: Observation with strict input output monitoring and repeat serum cortisol at 8 am the following day before commencing any glucocorticoid replacement to avoid confounding the diagnostic biochemistry today
options.rationale: Adrenal crisis is a clinical diagnosis and treatment is empirical before confirmation; delay for a morning cortisol risks death.

options.text: IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg over 24 hours infusion, IV normal saline 1000 mL over first hour, IV 10 percent dextrose 500 mL for hypoglycaemia and hold the levothyroxine dose today
options.rationale: Hyperpigmentation with hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and hypotension in a woman with autoimmune thyroid disease is primary adrenal insufficiency (Addison) in crisis; empirical hydrocortisone before biochemical confirmation is life-saving.

explanation.summary: Primary adrenal insufficiency in crisis presents with hypotension, hyponatraemia, hyperkalaemia, hypoglycaemia and hyperpigmentation from ACTH excess. Autoimmune polyglandular syndrome (with Hashimoto thyroiditis) is a classical association. Immediate management is IV hydrocortisone 100 mg stat then 200 mg over 24 hours infusion, IV normal saline for volume, dextrose for hypoglycaemia and treat any precipitant. Levothyroxine is held until glucocorticoid replacement is established to prevent worsening the crisis.
key_points: Hyperpigmentation + hyponatraemia + hyperkalaemia = primary adrenal insufficiency
IV hydrocortisone stat then 24 hr infusion is life-saving
Normal saline not Hartmann; dextrose for hypoglycaemia
Hold levothyroxine until glucocorticoid replacement established
explanation.pearls: Short synacthen test (250 microgram synthetic ACTH with cortisol at 0 and 30 min, expecting a peak above 500 nmol/L) confirms the diagnosis when done at least 24 hours after any hydrocortisone dose or by using dexamethasone as bridging therapy in the interim to avoid interference.

stem: A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes presents to your emergency department with 24 hours of severe left leg pain out of proportion to the visible skin appearance. He fell in the garden 3 days ago with a small abrasion to his left shin. Today the leg is swollen with a small area of erythema over the shin. His HR is 128, BP 96/60, temperature 39.2 C. He is confused and cold peripherally. On palpation there is crepitus over the calf and pain extending well beyond the visible erythema.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 96/60, RR 26, SpO2 96 percent, temp 39.2 C, cap refill 4 seconds, GCS 13
data_table.Examination: Small erythematous patch over shin with a 5 mm scab; pain and swelling extending well beyond visible erythema; crepitus on palpation of calf; foot cool with intact pulses; no bullae yet
data_table.Investigations: WCC 22 x10^9/L (4 to 11), CRP 285 mg/L (<5), Na 128 mmol/L (135 to 145), creatinine 168 micromol/L (<110), glucose 15.6 mmol/L, Hb 118 g/L, lactate 4.2 mmol/L (<2), CK 890 U/L (<200)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Urgent surgical consultation for wide debridement in theatre within 1 hour, IV meropenem 1 g and IV clindamycin 900 mg empirically, IV fluid resuscitation and blood cultures without delaying surgery
options.rationale: Pain out of proportion, crepitus, systemic toxicity and LRINEC-high biochemistry (WCC, Na, CRP, glucose, creatinine, Hb) in a diabetic point strongly to necrotising fasciitis; surgery within an hour is the intervention that improves survival.

options.text: IV flucloxacillin 2 g every 6 hours for standard cellulitis, IV normal saline 500 mL bolus, elevate the leg and mark the erythema border for reassessment in 4 hours before deciding on any further imaging
options.rationale: Cellulitis regimen misses the surgical urgency of necrotising fasciitis; pain out of proportion, crepitus and systemic toxicity mandate immediate surgical exploration.

options.text: CT lower limb with IV contrast to confirm gas in tissue planes before surgical consultation, with commencement of vancomycin and cefepime broad-spectrum antibiotics once radiological confirmation is obtained
options.rationale: Imaging must not delay surgery in suspected necrotising fasciitis; clinical diagnosis warrants immediate theatre for debridement and empirical antibiotics simultaneously.

options.text: Hyperbaric oxygen therapy referral as adjunctive treatment before surgical debridement is performed, with IV benzylpenicillin monotherapy for suspected clostridial gas gangrene from the garden wound
options.rationale: HBOT is adjunctive after debridement, not before; delay of surgery to arrange HBOT costs lives, and monotherapy misses the polymicrobial nature of type I necrotising fasciitis.

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g monotherapy with tetanus booster and topical mupirocin to the abrasion, planned admission to the medical ward for observation and outpatient surgical review within 48 hours if the pain persists
options.rationale: Ceftriaxone monotherapy does not cover the polymicrobial spectrum or provide clindamycin's antitoxin effect; and ward observation delays life-saving debridement.

explanation.summary: Necrotising fasciitis is a surgical emergency: features include pain out of proportion to examination, systemic toxicity, crepitus and haemorrhagic bullae later. LRINEC scoring supports suspicion using CRP, WCC, sodium, creatinine, haemoglobin and glucose. Management is immediate surgical exploration and wide debridement within 1 hour, empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics (meropenem plus clindamycin for antitoxin effect), IV fluid resuscitation and ICU-level supportive care. Imaging must never delay surgery.
key_points: Pain out of proportion + crepitus + systemic toxicity = suspect necrotising fasciitis
Surgical debridement within 1 hour is the priority
Empirical meropenem + clindamycin (antitoxin)
Never delay surgery for imaging
explanation.pearls: Add IV vancomycin if MRSA is prevalent in the community or hospital, and IV benzylpenicillin plus clindamycin for suspected group A streptococcal cases (LRINEC does not distinguish types); definitive antibiotics narrow once operative cultures return.

subtopic_detail: Type A aortic dissection recognition and initial management
stem: A 64-year-old man with a history of poorly controlled hypertension presents to your emergency department with 45 minutes of sudden severe tearing chest pain radiating to his back. He is diaphoretic and looks unwell. On examination his right arm BP is 178/98 and left arm BP is 128/72. He has a soft early diastolic murmur at the left sternal edge. ECG shows sinus rhythm with 1 mm ST depression in V4 to V6 without ST elevation. Bedside troponin is mildly elevated at 42 ng/L (<14).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 178/98 right arm and 128/72 left arm, RR 22, SpO2 96 percent, temp 36.8 C
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, alert; soft early diastolic murmur at LSE; right radial pulse full, left radial reduced volume; symmetrical lower limb pulses; no focal neurology
data_table.Investigations: ECG sinus rhythm, 1 mm ST depression V4 to V6, no STE; troponin 42 ng/L (<14); chest X-ray widened mediastinum >8 cm; VBG pH 7.34, lactate 2.4 mmol/L (<2); creatinine 108 micromol/L (<110)

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV sodium nitroprusside infusion titrated to systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg first, then IV metoprolol 5 mg boluses for rate control, plus IV aspirin 300 mg and heparin 5000 units for acute coronary syndrome
options.rationale: Vasodilator alone increases reflex tachycardia and worsens aortic wall shear stress; beta-blockade must be given first. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant are contraindicated in suspected dissection.

options.text: IV labetalol infusion titrated to HR 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg first before any vasodilator, urgent CT aortogram, cardiothoracic surgical activation, and hold antiplatelet or anticoagulant therapy for now
options.rationale: The tearing pain, inter-arm BP differential, aortic regurgitation murmur and widened mediastinum are classical type A aortic dissection; the AU order is negative chronotrope and beta-blockade before vasodilator to reduce shear (dP/dt), urgent CT and cardiothoracic activation.

options.text: Immediate cardiac catheterisation for suspected NSTEMI given the ST depression, elevated troponin and chest pain, deferring aortic imaging until angiography excludes an acute coronary syndrome first
options.rationale: Angiography and anticoagulation on this NSTE presentation would kill a dissection patient; a widened mediastinum and inter-arm BP differential warrant aortogram before cath.

options.text: IV hydralazine 20 mg bolus every 20 minutes for BP control, oral aspirin 300 mg loading, oral clopidogrel 300 mg loading and admit to the coronary care unit for continuous cardiac monitoring overnight
options.rationale: Hydralazine increases reflex tachycardia and shear stress in dissection; and antiplatelet loading is contraindicated. Beta-blockade first, not hydralazine.

options.text: Thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg IV over 90 minutes for suspected STEMI equivalent posterior wall infarction given the persistent ST depression V4 to V6 in this high risk chest pain presentation today
options.rationale: Thrombolysis in an unrecognised dissection is invariably fatal; the ST depression here reflects demand ischaemia from coronary compromise or dissection propagation, not STEMI equivalent that meets criteria.

explanation.summary: Type A aortic dissection presents with abrupt tearing chest and back pain, inter-arm blood pressure differential, aortic regurgitation from proximal extension, widened mediastinum on chest X-ray and pulse deficits. Immediate management is IV beta-blockade (labetalol or esmolol) titrated to HR 60 and systolic BP 100 to 120 mmHg before any vasodilator to minimise dP/dt and aortic wall shear stress; urgent CT aortogram and cardiothoracic surgical activation. Antiplatelet and anticoagulant therapy is held pending imaging. Definitive management of type A is emergency open surgical repair.
key_points: Tearing pain + inter-arm BP differential + widened mediastinum = suspect dissection
Beta-blockade FIRST (target HR 60), then vasodilator (target SBP 100 to 120)
Urgent CT aortogram and cardiothoracic activation
Withhold antiplatelet and anticoagulant pending diagnosis
explanation.pearls: Type A dissection (involving the ascending aorta) is a surgical emergency with mortality rising 1 percent per hour; type B (descending only, distal to left subclavian) is managed medically unless complicated by malperfusion, rupture or refractory pain and hypertension, when thoracic endovascular aortic repair is considered.
